_comment: TEXTS REGISTRY. Every text on the timeline is registered here by ID with its scholarly date range, a credible source, and either an imported copy (data/texts/<id>.txt) or an external link. Timeline events in the per-tradition files reference these IDs. Dates are BCE years; from > to (older first). Never present disputed dates as settled — use the certainty field.

content.label: Read the UCL overview and translations

date_range.note: First Intermediate Period through the Middle Kingdom; painted inside non-royal coffins.

coffin-texts.source_label: UCL Digital Egypt for Universities — Coffin Texts
coffin-texts.title: Coffin Texts
coffin-texts.what: Some 1,185 funerary spells adapting Pyramid Texts material for non-royal dead — the afterlife democratized — and introducing the judgment of the dead before Osiris.

content.label: Read the Gathas, tr. L. H. Mills (1898, public domain PDF)

date_range.note: No scholarly consensus. Linguistic parallels with the Rig Veda point to the mid-to-late 2nd millennium BCE (Boyce, Hintze); other scholars allow dates as late as the 6th century BCE.

gathas.title: Gathas of Zarathustra
gathas.what: 17 hymns in Old Avestan traditionally attributed to Zarathustra himself — the oldest layer of the Avesta. They preach one Wise Lord (Ahura Mazda), the choice between truth (asha) and the lie (druj), and individual judgment after death.

content.label: Scholarly discussion (cuneiform text held by the Oxford ETCSL corpus)

date_range.note: Earliest tablets from Abu Salabikh (Early Dynastic IIIa); the text was copied in scribal schools for over a millennium, so later copies do not date the composition.

instructions-of-shuruppak.source_label: N. Samet, 'The Sumerian proverb collections' — on the Early Dynastic Instructions of Shuruppak (ResearchGate)
instructions-of-shuruppak.title: Instructions of Shuruppak
instructions-of-shuruppak.what: One of the oldest known works of wisdom literature: proverbial instructions from King Shuruppak to his son Ziusudra, the Sumerian flood hero.

date_range.note: Late Shang dynasty, Anyang (Yinxu); Wu Ding-era bones radiocarbon dated to 1254–1197 BCE.

oracle-bone-inscriptions.source_label: Indiana University ScholarWorks — Glossed Texts for the Study of Shang Oracle Bone Inscriptions
oracle-bone-inscriptions.title: Oracle-bone inscriptions
oracle-bone-inscriptions.what: Divination records carved on ox scapulae and turtle plastrons — the earliest Chinese writing. Shang kings queried ancestors and high gods about harvests, warfare, and ritual.

date_range.note: Inscribed in the pyramids of Unas (24th c. BCE) through the 6th Dynasty at Saqqara; internal evidence suggests some spells preserve older oral material.

pyramid-texts.source_label: Internet Sacred Text Archive — The Pyramid Texts, tr. Samuel A. B. Mercer (1952)
pyramid-texts.title: Pyramid Texts
pyramid-texts.what: Funerary spells inscribed on the walls of Old Kingdom royal pyramids — the oldest extensive religious literature from ancient Egypt, guiding the king's ascent to the afterlife.

date_range.note: Scholarly consensus (Flood, Witzel, Anthony) places the bulk of the hymns c. 1500–1200 BCE; some scholars widen the range to 1700–1100 BCE. Composed orally, committed to writing much later.

rig-veda.source_label: Internet Sacred Text Archive — Rig Veda, tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith (1896)
rig-veda.title: Rig Veda
rig-veda.what: 1,028 hymns in Vedic Sanskrit by priestly families of the Sapta-Sindhu region, preserved by exacting oral transmission. Centers on rta (cosmic order), sacrifice, and gods such as Indra and Agni.

date_range.note: 305 poems dated from the 11th to 7th centuries BCE; the collection was traditionally said to have been edited by Confucius.

shijing.source_label: Internet Archive — The She King, tr. James Legge (1871), scanned from the Chinese Classics
shijing.title: Shijing (Classic of Poetry)
shijing.what: The oldest collection of Chinese poetry: folk songs, court odes, and temple hymns including sacrificial odes to royal ancestors. Became one of the Confucian Five Classics.

date_range.note: Attributed to Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad (c. 2334–2279 BCE) and high priestess of Nanna at Ur; authorship is traditional rather than proven.

temple-hymns-enheduanna.source_label: Jacket2 (University of Pennsylvania) — commentary and translation by Betty De Shong Meador
temple-hymns-enheduanna.title: Temple Hymns of Enheduanna
temple-hymns-enheduanna.what: 42 hymns addressed to the temples of Sumer, attributed to Enheduanna — the earliest named author in world literature.

date_range.note: Core Zhouyi layers built up during the Western Zhou; exact stratification is debated. The Ten Wings commentaries are later (Warring States/Han).

yijing.source_label: Internet Sacred Text Archive — The Yî King, tr. James Legge (1882)
yijing.title: Yijing (I Ching / Book of Changes)
yijing.what: A divination manual of 64 hexagrams with judgments and line statements, later expanded into a cosmology of change.
